seven_q.Q0_posture: Analytical and synthetic; the document assumes that formal impossibility results in mathematics and physics have structural implications for theology, and that these domains can be mapped isomorphically.
seven_q.Q1_identity: An isomorphism record (ISO-002) that maps six impossibility theorems from mathematics and physics to five properties of grace in Christian theology.
seven_q.Q2_domain: Lives at the intersection of mathematics, physics, information theory, philosophy, and Christian theology; primarily a structural isomorphism document.
seven_q.Q3_claim: Closed systems are structurally incapable of self-rescue; any coherent rescue must have five specific properties (externality, sufficiency, asymmetric cost, merit-independence, temporal priority); Christian grace has exactly these properties.
seven_q.Q4_support: Six independent theorems (Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Clausius, Landauer, Leibniz) each demonstrate a specific impossibility for closed systems; the five grace properties are the logical inversions of these impossibilities; the mapping passes the swap test.
seven_q.Q5_dependencies: Depends on the validity of the six theorems (all well-established), the definition of grace in Ephesians 2:8-9, and the assumption that structural isomorphisms between domains are meaningful.
seven_q.Q6_consequences: Forces the conclusion that Pelagianism and semi-Pelagianism are structurally incoherent; constrains soteriology to require all five grace properties; predicts that no closed system will ever achieve self-validation; reframes the alignment problem as a Gödelian constraint.
seven_q.Q7_kill: Breaking any one of the six theorems (e.g., finding a closed system that proves its own consistency) would remove the necessity of the corresponding grace property; breaking all six would eliminate the structural necessity for grace entirely.
